newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Handelsbanken half year profits up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Handelsbanken half year profits up.

text.p: Sweden's largest commercial bank Svenska Handelsbanken reported on Tuesday a healthy lift in half-year profits, hinting that it could be a key bidder for the state's 34 percent stake in mortgage institute Stadshypotek.
Handelsbanken's 3.00 billion crowns ($455.6 million) profit after loan losses for the first half of the year was 17 percent up on the 2.57 billion crowns posted in the same 1995 period.

Always the strongest of the Swedish banks during the credit crisis of the early 1990s, Handelsbanken's loan losses did not have as far to fall as those of competitors such as S-E-Banken and Nordbanken.

At 892 million crowns, Handelsbanken's net loan losses for the first half of the year corresponded to 0.6 percent of total lending volumes, a return to levels prevailing before the spectacular property and banking crashes of the first years of this decade.
Handelsbanken president Arne Martensson said there was every chance of loan losses dwindling further.

"Non-performing loans continue to decline, and we have a lower level of non-performers than other (Swedish) banks. This indicates that credit losses will continue falling," Martensson told a news conference.

But falling loan losses were by no means the only source of improved profits for the bank. Higher lending volume led to a two percent increase in net interest income to 4.72 billion crowns, despite a squeeze on margins from intensifying competition.

A boom year for the Swedish stock market also made its mark on Handelsbanken's top line. Commission income rose 29 percent to 1.64 billion crowns on a wave of higher brokerage volumes and corporate finance transactions.

"Since 1993, Handelsbanken has continually strengthened its trading position on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, and was the leading participant in the first and second quarters of 1996," the bank said in a statement.
Costs increased by 10 percent, of which three percentage points were attributable to higher depreciation in the leasing operations of the group's financing unit.

With all of the Swedish commercial banks back on a sound footing, Handelsbanken is widely tipped as a leader in what many analysts expect will be a process of dog-eat-dog in the Nordic banking sector.

Freed of the dual millstones of credit losses and the property holdings taken over as collateral during the crisis year, cash-rich Swedish banks are not just potential predators -- their bulging coffers also make them attractive targets.

Handelsbanken is too large a morsel for any other Swedish bank to swallow, but Martensson said the bank could be in the bidding for the state's expected sale of its 34 percent holding in mortgage institute Stadshypotek.
"I can't rule out the possibilty that we'll be in the bidding for Stadshypotek," he said, adding that he saw the institute as a natural complement to Handelsbanken's operations in the area.
